adversarial_test_results.prompt: The archive of the municipal conservatory had remained sealed for nearly forty years, and the staff who finally opened it on a rainy Tuesday in March were not prepared for what they found. Shelves of manuscripts, letters and concert programmes filled three rooms, and the dust rose in clouds whenever a box was moved. The earliest documents dated from the founding of the institute, when a handful of teachers taught harmony and counterpoint to students who paid in coin. Over the following weeks the collection was sorted, catalogued and photographed, and by the end of the summer a rough inventory had been typed up and circulated among the faculty. Many of the letters were ordinary business: requests for instruments, complaints about heating, notes about rehearsals that had been cancelled because of snow. Others were more surprising, including a long correspondence with a publisher in Leipzig who had promised to print a series of chamber works and then quietly abandoned the project after the first volume sold poorly. The correspondence also contains a number of photographs, some of them annotated on the back with names and dates that have since been identified. A few of the letters mention a dispute between two professors over the correct tempo of a well known symphony, a quarrel that apparently divided the faculty for an entire season. The catalogue itself was assembled by R. Halvorsen, a librarian who had joined the staff only two years earlier and who worked through the boxes with remarkable patience. He noted the condition of every item, flagged the pages that had been damaged by damp, and traced the provenance of several manuscripts back to the estates of families who had left the city in the previous century. His notes, written in a small careful hand, are now kept alongside the collection. Visitors who wish to consult the archive must write in advance, and the reading room, which overlooks the old courtyard, is open on weekday afternoons. The director hopes that a complete edition of the letters will appear within the next few years, though the funding for such a project has not yet been secured. In the meantime, the staff continue to answer enquiries from scholars in other countries, and a small exhibition of the most interesting items is planned for the autumn. A short guide, prepared for the opening, summarises the history of the building and describes the most fragile volumes in the collection.
